title: Frogs Wear Invisible Bacteria Armor to Fight Deadly Fungus
summary: What if you had a suit of armor made of tiny living creatures? Some frogs do! Scientists have discovered that certain tropical frogs survive a deadly fungus because of bacteria living on their skin. The fungus, called chytrid (Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis), has already wiped out at least 90 frog species. It attacks frog skin, causing damage and eventually heart failure. But some frogs have a secret weapon: their skin microbiome — a community of bacteria that acts like a shield. "This is one of the clearest demonstrations that a host's natural skin bacteria can be a frontline defense against a pathogen," said Gui Becker, a biologist at Penn State University. In a lab in Brazil, researchers studied two frog species. One, Haddadus binotatus, usually survives the fungus in the wild. But when scientists used antibiotics to remove its skin bacteria, it became more likely to get sick. The other species, Ischnocnema henselii, was highly susceptible even with its bacteria. "We see this striking contrast: one species has one of the highest prevalences of the fungus, while the other has no infections in the wild," said Laura Schuck, a study co-author. The team cultured about 700 strains of bacteria from frog skin and tested which ones stopped the fungus from growing. They built a database linking each bacterium to its protective power. In the future, they hope to learn how frogs get these helpful bacteria from their environment. "If we understand how this frog recruits and maintains beneficial bacteria, we can begin to understand how the microbiome works as a natural defense," Schuck said.
why_it_matters: This story shows that the tiniest living things — bacteria too small to see — can protect bigger animals, and it reminds us that losing frog species would harm the ponds and wetlands in our own neighbourhoods.

background_read: The chytrid fungus is one of the worst wildlife diseases ever recorded, and it has harmed hundreds of kinds of frogs and other amphibians around the world.
Frogs have thin, wet skin that they use to breathe and to soak up water, which is why a disease that attacks skin is so dangerous for them.
Scientists believe the fungus spread to new countries when people moved frogs around the world for pets, food and research.
Article_Structure: WHO: Biologists including Gui Becker of Penn State University and Laura Schuck, studying two Brazilian frog species
WHAT: They found that bacteria living on frog skin can act like a shield against the deadly chytrid fungus, and built a database of which bacteria work best
WHERE: A laboratory in Brazil, using frogs that live in the wild there
WHY: Understanding how frogs recruit helpful skin bacteria could help scientists protect amphibians from a fungus that has already wiped out many species

perspectives.description: They see frog skin bacteria as a natural defense that might one day help save amphibians from a fungus that has already killed off many species.
They warn that the fungus is still spreading and that many frogs do not have protective bacteria at all, so some species may disappear before we understand them.
They point out that lab tests are not the same as life in the wild, and that scientists still do not know how frogs actually pick up these helpful bacteria.
